summary: Qualifiers like "in-band" and "out-of-band" get prepended to OAM, and the same qualifier is understood differently in different contexts. This Best Current Practice gives guidelines for using such terms precisely. It updates RFC 6291.

plainLanguage.summary: People use the same word to mean different things, so this tells them how to say exactly what they mean.

questions: why avoid in-band and out-of-band oam
subtitle: Stop saying "in-band" and "out-of-band" about OAM; use precise terms for how OAM behaves instead.

tldr.problem: Qualifiers such as "in-band" and "out-of-band" come from radio and telephony, where a real band exists. In packet networks the same words are read in different ways in different documents.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends avoiding both terms for OAM and defines replacements along three criteria: Active, Passive or Hybrid mode (including In-Data-Packet OAM), Path-Congruent or not, and Equal or Different Forwarding Treatment.
tldr.outcome: IETF documents that qualify the term OAM SHOULD use these definitions, and authors can point to this RFC with a template sentence. It extends RFC 6291 without modifying it.

today: RFC 10014 is a Best Current Practice published in June 2026. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it extends RFC 6291 without changing it.

sections.title: Why In-Band and Out-of-Band Are Confusing
sections.content:
The terms in-band and out-of-band were used extensively in radio communications and in telephony signaling. There, an actual band (a channel or frequency) exists to be within or outside.

IP and packet-switched networks have no band as such, and have multiple things OAM traffic can be carried within or outside of. A frequent case is the use of in-band to mean either in-data-packet or on-path. Examples in existing RFCs, such as VCCV (RFC 5085) and OAM for Deterministic Networking (RFC 9551), use the term with different meanings. The RFC concludes that within the IETF the terms cannot be reliably understood consistently and unambiguously, and that they cannot be understood by someone seeing them for the first time. It does not change the meaning of terms in any prior RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: "In-band" comes from radio, where you can be inside or outside a channel. The internet has no such channel, so people ended up using the word for several different ideas.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
The RFC recommends avoiding the terms "in-band" and "out-of-band" when referring to OAM. It encourages more fine-grained, descriptive terminology instead, and presents alternative terms for future IETF documents about OAM. Other precise terms that do not rely on the "-band" convention are not ruled out.

The new terminology classifies OAM by three criteria: whether it is active, passive or hybrid; whether it follows the same path as data traffic; and whether it receives the same treatment as data traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not say "in-band". Instead, say exactly what you mean: how the check is done, which road it takes, and whether it is treated like normal traffic.

sections.title: Active, Passive and Hybrid OAM
sections.content:
These terms are consistent with RFC 7799.

  • Active OAM uses dedicated OAM packets.
  • Passive OAM relies on observing existing data packet streams, uses no dedicated OAM packets and does not modify data packets.
  • Hybrid OAM combines active and passive methods, and may augment or modify the stream of interest. RFC 7799 distinguishes Hybrid Type I (one stream of interest) from Hybrid Type II (two or more).

The RFC defines In-Data-Packet OAM as a specific case of Hybrid OAM (and of Hybrid Type I) in which OAM information is carried in the packets that also carry the data traffic. It was sometimes called "in-band".

Examples: MPLS echo request/reply messages are Active; counting packets in a stream is Passive; an IOAM trace option in data packets, and Alternate Marking applied to a single stream, are Hybrid Type I and In-Data-Packet. Direct Loss Measurement is Hybrid Type I but not In-Data-Packet, because user packets are not modified.
sections.plainLanguage: Active is like sending a test messenger. Passive is like just watching the cars go by. Hybrid mixes the two, and "in-data-packet" means writing a note on the cars themselves.

sections.title: Path and Forwarding Treatment
sections.content:
Path-Congruent OAM follows the exact same forwarding path as the observed data traffic. Non-Path-Congruent OAM is not guaranteed to. Path-congruent packets traverse the same nodes and links, but this says nothing about how they are treated in queues. VCCV Type 1, once called "In-Band VCCV", is an example of Path-Congruent OAM.

Equal-Forwarding-Treatment OAM receives the same forwarding treatment (for example QoS) as user data packets; Different-Forwarding-Treatment OAM might not. When both path and treatment match, the OAM packets are said to exhibit fate-sharing with the data, so any impairment affecting the data is reflected in the OAM results. Without that, measurements and diagnostics can mislead and corrective actions can be inadequate. RFC 9551 calls this property "In-band OAM".
sections.plainLanguage: Path-congruent means the test messenger takes the same road as the cars. Equal treatment means it also waits in the same traffic jams. Then what it learns is what the cars experience.

sections.title: Combining the Criteria
sections.content:
Not every criterion applies to every mechanism, and not every combination is possible. Passive OAM sends no dedicated packets, so path and treatment do not apply. Non-Path-Congruent OAM cannot be Equal-Forwarding-Treatment. The RFC suggests classifying a mechanism first as Active, Passive or Hybrid/In-Data-Packet, and then considering the other two criteria case by case.

Worked examples: IP Ping (ICMP Echo) is Active, Non-Path-Congruent and Different-Forwarding-Treatment. An IOAM trace option in data packets is In-Data-Packet, Path-Congruent and Equal-Forwarding-Treatment. VCCV is Active, Path-Congruent and Different-Forwarding-Treatment. MPLS Inferred Loss Measurement is Active and Path-Congruent, and can be either Equal- or Different-Forwarding-Treatment.

Measurement protocols need Path-Congruence and Equal-Forwarding-Treatment for accurate results, but other OAM protocols do not. BFD control packets are often sent with the highest priority, so they do not follow Equal-Forwarding-Treatment.
sections.plainLanguage: You can describe any check using the three questions. Some questions do not apply: if you only watch cars, you have no messenger to ask about.

sections.title: Applicability and Conformance
sections.content:
IETF documents qualifying the term OAM SHOULD use these definitions. Documents that want other characterizations can introduce them, as long as the terms differ from those defined here.

Authors who follow these terms SHOULD add a sentence, typically in the terminology section, saying that the listed OAM terms are to be interpreted as described in RFC 10014. The RFC supplies the template text for this.
sections.plainLanguage: If you use these names in your document, add a note saying where they come from, so readers know exactly what they mean.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security is improved when terms are used with precision and their definitions are unambiguous. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: When everyone uses words the same way, there are fewer mix-ups, and fewer mix-ups means fewer mistakes.
